title: Collagen Synthesis — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Structural Proteins: Collagen & Elastin lecture (Edwin F. Laing) and study guide

questions.stem: What is the principal mechanical function of collagen in connective tissue?
questions.why: Collagen fibrils are strong under tension. Their triple-helical molecules and intermolecular cross-links help tissues such as tendons and skin resist being pulled apart.

notes.A: ATP production is a cellular metabolic function rather than a mechanical role of extracellular collagen.
notes.C: Lipid oxidation requires metabolic enzymes, and collagen serves as a structural protein.
notes.D: Membrane glucose transport relies on specialised transporters rather than extracellular collagen fibres.
notes.E: Endocrine cells secrete hormones, whereas collagen is deposited to support tissue structure.

questions.stem: Which cell is the major source of collagen and ground substance in connective tissue proper?
questions.why: Fibroblasts are the main matrix-producing cells in connective tissue proper. They secrete collagens and other proteins as well as components of the hydrated ground substance.

notes.A: Mature erythrocytes transport oxygen and lack the organelles needed to synthesise and secrete matrix proteins.
notes.B: Platelets release mediators and clotting proteins during haemostasis, rather than laying down the bulk of ordinary connective tissue matrix.
notes.C: Schwann cells support peripheral axons and can make basal lamina, but they are not the principal matrix cells of connective tissue proper.
notes.D: Hepatocytes make many plasma proteins. In the liver, stellate cells are important sources of collagen, especially during fibrosis.

questions.stem: Which transmembrane proteins physically link extracellular matrix proteins to the intracellular cytoskeleton?
questions.why: Integrins have extracellular domains that bind matrix ligands and cytoplasmic tails that recruit proteins linked to the cytoskeleton. This couples cell adhesion to mechanical signalling.

notes.A: Selectins mediate transient carbohydrate-dependent cell adhesion, such as leukocyte rolling along endothelium.
notes.B: Classical cadherins link the cytoskeleton to neighbouring cells through cell–cell junctions.
notes.D: Claudins form tight-junction strands between adjacent cells and regulate paracellular permeability.
notes.E: Connexins assemble gap junction channels that permit exchange of small molecules between neighbouring cells.

questions.stem: Which extracellular protein prominently helps cells adhere to the surrounding matrix?
questions.why: Fibronectin is a matrix glycoprotein that binds cellular integrins and matrix components such as collagen. It thereby helps attach the cell surface to extracellular matrix.

notes.B: Haemoglobin is an erythrocyte protein that carries oxygen in blood.
notes.C: Troponin regulates striated muscle contraction in response to calcium.
notes.D: Transferrin transports iron in plasma rather than bridging cells to matrix.
notes.E: Myoglobin binds oxygen within muscle cells and has no principal extracellular adhesion role.

questions.stem: Which collagen type predominates in bone, skin and tendons?
questions.why: Type I is the major fibril-forming collagen of bone, skin, tendons and ligaments.

notes.A: Type II is the major fibril-forming collagen of most cartilage and is also found in the vitreous.
notes.B: Type III forms reticular fibres and often accompanies type I in skin and vascular connective tissue.
notes.C: Type IV forms networks in basal laminae instead of the main load-bearing fibrils of these tissues.
notes.E: Type VII forms anchoring fibrils beneath certain epithelia, rather than most of the tensile matrix in bone or tendon.

questions.stem: Which collagen type is especially characteristic of cartilage and vitreous humour?
questions.why: Type II collagen forms the main fibrils of hyaline cartilage and is a major component of vitreous collagen fibrils.

notes.A: Type I forms the principal tensile fibrils of tendon, skin and bone.
notes.C: Type III is a major component of reticular fibres in vascular and stromal connective tissues.
notes.D: Type IV forms networks that reinforce basal laminae rather than cartilage fibrils.
notes.E: Type V regulates fibril assembly and is commonly associated with type I fibrils.

questions.stem: Which collagen type is found prominently in blood-vessel walls and reticular connective tissue?
questions.why: Type III collagen forms reticular fibres that support blood vessels and many organs. It commonly occurs alongside type I in extensible tissues.

notes.A: Type I is abundant in many vessel walls, but type III is characteristic of the reticular fibres named in the stem.
notes.B: Type II is characteristic of cartilage rather than the supporting reticular network of blood vessels.
notes.C: Type IV is found in vascular basal laminae, where it forms a sheet-like network rather than reticular fibres.
notes.D: Type VII forms anchoring fibrils at certain epithelial basement membranes.

questions.stem: Which collagen type forms sheet-like networks in the basal lamina?
questions.why: Type IV collagen molecules associate into a flexible network in the basal lamina. This sheet-like scaffold differs structurally from the long fibrils of types I, II and III.

notes.A: Type I forms load-bearing fibrils, such as those in tendon and bone.
notes.B: Type II forms cartilage fibrils rather than the principal basal-lamina network.
notes.D: Type III is a fibril-forming collagen associated with reticular fibres.
notes.E: Type V usually co-assembles with other fibrillar collagens and regulates fibril size.

questions.stem: Which collagen type forms anchoring fibrils beneath stratified squamous epithelia?
questions.why: Type VII collagen assembles into anchoring fibrils that link the epithelial basement membrane to underlying connective tissue. This attachment helps resist shear at sites such as the skin.

notes.B: Type IX associates with type II fibrils in cartilage rather than forming epithelial anchoring fibrils.
notes.C: Type XII is a fibril-associated collagen found on fibril surfaces, rather than the main polymer of anchoring fibrils.
notes.D: Type XVII is a transmembrane collagen in hemidesmosomes, whereas anchoring fibrils are extracellular assemblies of type VII.
notes.E: Type XVIII is a basement-membrane collagen and the precursor of endostatin, rather than the main component of anchoring fibrils.

questions.stem: Which collagen type laterally associates with type II fibrils in cartilage?
questions.why: Type IX is a fibril-associated collagen that lies on the surface of cartilage fibrils containing type II. Its projecting domains can interact with surrounding matrix.

notes.A: Type I forms the principal fibrils of tendon, bone and other tensile connective tissues.
notes.B: Type III forms reticular fibrils and is often associated with type I in other tissues.
notes.C: Type IV forms basal-lamina networks rather than the characteristic surface coat of cartilage type II fibrils.
notes.E: Type VII forms anchoring fibrils below certain epithelial basement membranes.

questions.stem: How many alpha polypeptide chains form a tropocollagen triple helix?
questions.why: Three collagen alpha chains wind around one another to form the triple-helical tropocollagen molecule. The individual chains may have identical or different sequences depending on collagen type.

notes.A: Two chains would constitute a dimer, which lacks the third strand needed for collagen's triple helix.
notes.C: A fourth chain is not part of the individual tropocollagen molecule even when molecules later assemble into fibrils.
notes.D: Collagen fibrils contain multiple molecules, but the individual helix is assembled from fewer than five chains.
notes.E: Two triple-helical molecules together contain six chains. One tropocollagen molecule has only three.

questions.stem: What proportion of collagen amino acid residues is approximately glycine?
questions.why: Glycine occupies every third position in the triple-helical Gly–X–Y repeat. It therefore makes up roughly one third of residues in the helical region.

notes.A: One in five would be too sparse to place glycine at every third position needed at the helix core.
notes.B: One in four is incompatible with the Gly–X–Y repeat, which has three positions.
notes.C: One in six would occupy only half the regularly spaced glycine positions in an ideal helix.
notes.D: One in seven is inconsistent with the repeated insertion of a glycine every three residues.

questions.stem: Why must glycine occur frequently in the collagen triple helix?

options.label: B
options.text: It is the source of bound vitamin C

options.label: C
options.text: Its small side chain fits the core

questions.why: Glycine has a hydrogen atom as its side chain. At every third position its small size permits the three alpha chains to pack tightly around the axis.

notes.A: Disulphide bonds require cysteine residues, and glycine has no sulphur-containing side chain.
notes.B: Ascorbate helps collagen hydroxylation but does not come from any glycine residue.
notes.D: Intermolecular covalent cross-links involve lysine or hydroxylysine derivatives rather than glycine side chains.
notes.E: Glycine's size permits tight packing compatible with interchain hydrogen bonds that stabilise the helix.

questions.stem: Which amino acid triplet is commonly repeated in collagen polypeptide chains?
questions.why: The triple-helical collagen sequence repeats Gly–X–Y. Proline commonly occupies the X position and hydroxyproline often occupies Y, making this a representative triplet.

notes.B: The three hydrophobic residues lack the glycine needed at each repeated position near the helix axis.
notes.C: This group of hydroxyl-containing amino acids does not contain the obligatory glycine of the collagen triplet.
notes.D: Charged residues may occur at variable positions, but the listed triplet does not supply the repeated glycine.
notes.E: Sulphur-containing or histidine residues can occur in proteins, but this set lacks the core glycine of the collagen repeat.

questions.stem: Which modified amino acid particularly contributes to collagen triple-helix thermal stability?
questions.why: In helical collagen, 4-hydroxyproline favours conformations that stabilise the triple helix at body temperature. Impaired proline hydroxylation can therefore yield a less stable helix.

notes.A: Lysine modifications have roles in collagen processing, but methyllysine is not the main residue providing this helical stability.
notes.B: Phosphoserine has roles in protein regulation and is not the relevant product of collagen hydroxylation.
notes.C: Cystine is a disulphide-linked pair of cysteines. Propeptide disulphides can aid chain alignment but do not account for the thermal effect in the helix.
notes.E: Glycine is essential for close packing, but acetylglycine is not the characteristic modified residue underlying this thermal stability.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces a glycine normally buried in a collagen helix with a bulky amino acid. What is most directly disrupted?

options.label: A
options.text: Initiation of fatty acid beta oxidation

options.label: B
options.text: Tight packing of the three chains

questions.why: The glycine side chain projects into a crowded part of the triple helix. A bulkier substitution interferes with chain packing and can delay folding or destabilise the collagen helix.

notes.A: Fatty acid beta oxidation uses metabolic enzymes and is not directly affected by steric crowding within a collagen helix.
notes.C: Nucleosomes contain histone proteins and DNA, rather than the three collagen alpha chains.
notes.D: Myoglobin stores oxygen in muscle using a haem group, a mechanism distinct from collagen assembly.
notes.E: Albumin's binding sites depend on albumin folding rather than the tight packing of collagen chains.

questions.stem: When are proline and lysine residues hydroxylated during collagen biosynthesis?
questions.why: Hydroxylation is a post-translational modification of proline and lysine residues before the stable triple helix assembles.

questions.stem: Which enzyme forms 4-hydroxyproline from selected proline residues of nascent collagen?
questions.why: Collagen prolyl 4-hydroxylase converts selected incorporated proline residues into 4-hydroxyproline. The ER enzyme uses oxygen, ferrous iron and alpha-ketoglutarate, with ascorbate supporting its activity.

notes.A: Lysyl oxidase modifies lysine side chains outside the cell to initiate covalent cross-linking.
notes.B: Procollagen peptidases remove terminal propeptides rather than hydroxylating proline residues.
notes.D: A galactosyltransferase attaches galactose to suitable acceptors such as hydroxylysine.
notes.E: Tyrosine hydroxylase acts on tyrosine in catecholamine synthesis rather than altering proline in collagen.

questions.stem: Which cofactor maintains the active-site iron of prolyl hydroxylase in its reduced functional state?
questions.why: Ascorbate supports iron-dependent collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases by maintaining active reduced iron.

notes.B: Biotin transfers carbon dioxide equivalents in carboxylase reactions rather than maintaining reduced iron in collagen hydroxylase.
notes.C: Cobalamin supports reactions such as methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and methionine synthase, not this collagen reaction.
notes.D: Riboflavin supplies flavin cofactors for various redox enzymes but is not the reductant specified here.
notes.E: Folate cofactors carry one-carbon units and do not keep this hydroxylase's iron in the ferrous form.

questions.stem: Which molecule is consumed alongside molecular oxygen during collagen proline hydroxylation?
questions.why: Prolyl hydroxylase couples hydroxylation to oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-ketoglutarate. One oxygen atom enters the modified proline side chain while alpha-ketoglutarate yields succinate and carbon dioxide.

notes.A: The reaction forms succinate, rather than consuming the distinct thioester succinyl-CoA.
notes.B: Malonyl-CoA supplies carbon for fatty acid synthesis and does not drive prolyl hydroxylation.
notes.C: Oxaloacetate is a citric acid cycle intermediate, but the hydroxylase specifically uses alpha-ketoglutarate.
notes.E: Acetylcarnitine has a role in handling acetyl groups rather than supplying the oxidised cosubstrate of this hydroxylase.

questions.stem: Why does an iron chelator such as alpha-alpha-bipyridyl destabilize newly synthesized collagen?
questions.why: Removal of available iron can inhibit collagen prolyl hydroxylase, an iron-dependent enzyme. Reduced hydroxyproline formation makes the triple helix less thermally stable.

notes.A: Lysyl oxidase requires copper and acts extracellularly in cross-linking rather than supplying hydroxyproline.
notes.C: Faster secretion would not restore helical stability when the proline residues are insufficiently hydroxylated.
notes.D: Chelation reduces hydroxylase activity. It does not improve the regular placement of glycine during translation.
notes.E: The immediate biochemical effect is on activity of an existing hydroxylase enzyme rather than transcription of collagen genes.

questions.stem: Which enzyme hydroxylates selected lysine side chains of nascent collagen?
questions.why: Lysyl hydroxylase modifies lysine before helix formation; lysyl oxidase acts later in extracellular cross-linking.

notes.A: Lysyl oxidase deaminates certain lysine and hydroxylysine residues extracellularly to initiate cross-linking.
notes.B: Histidine decarboxylase produces histamine rather than modifying lysine on nascent collagen.
notes.C: Prolyl hydroxylase modifies residues of proline, whereas the question asks about lysine.
notes.D: Argininosuccinate lyase acts in the urea cycle and has no collagen lysine hydroxylase activity.

questions.stem: Where are glucose and galactose residues attached during collagen processing?

options.label: B
options.text: To the unmodified proline side chains

questions.why: Collagen-directed glycosyltransferases attach galactose to selected hydroxylysine residues. A glucose can then be added to form glucosylgalactosylhydroxylysine.

notes.A: Unmodified glycine has no side-chain hydroxyl group to accept this carbohydrate.
notes.B: Proline can be hydroxylated, but unmodified proline is not the acceptor for this collagen glycosylation.
notes.D: Fibrinogen is a different extracellular protein and does not supply the glycosylation sites on collagen.
notes.E: Terminal cysteine disulphides can stabilise propeptide association, but collagen's characteristic sugars are attached to hydroxylysine.

questions.stem: Which collagen preparation is expected to show comparatively extensive carbohydrate substitution?
questions.why: Type IV collagen of basal laminae commonly contains many glycosylated hydroxylysines. Tendon type I collagen typically has much less carbohydrate substitution.

notes.B: Tendon type I collagen is a fibril-forming collagen with relatively low hydroxylysine glycosylation.
notes.C: Cartilage type II collagen is glycosylated, but the type IV network is a classic example of particularly extensive substitution.
notes.D: Vascular type III is fibril-forming and can be glycosylated, but basal-lamina type IV typically has more extensive substitution.
notes.E: Type VII has glycosylated sites, but its characteristic feature is anchoring fibril formation and it is not the usual example of high hydroxylysine glycosylation.

questions.stem: Why do procollagen terminal propeptides remain attached before secretion?

options.label: A
options.text: They replace the alpha chain backbone

questions.why: Terminal propeptides keep fibril-forming procollagen sufficiently soluble for intracellular processing and secretion. Their later removal allows the collagen molecules to assemble into fibrils.

notes.A: The propeptides are extensions of the chains, which already contain the central triple-helical domain.
notes.B: Calcium-dependent coagulation takes place through clotting factor complexes rather than procollagen propeptides.
notes.C: Ascorbate is supplied independently and its regeneration is not the function of the propeptides.
notes.E: Desmosine is a characteristic elastin cross-link, not the means by which procollagen avoids premature assembly.

questions.stem: Where are terminal procollagen propeptides normally removed to permit fibril assembly?
questions.why: Procollagen peptidases generally cleave the terminal propeptides during or after secretion into the extracellular matrix. This processing permits fibril-forming collagen molecules to pack together.

notes.A: The mitochondrial matrix is a site of oxidative metabolism rather than the usual site of procollagen maturation.
notes.C: Ribosomes synthesise the chains, but terminal cleavage for fibril formation involves specialised procollagen peptidases.
notes.D: Nuclear chromatin contains DNA and associated proteins rather than the site of secreted collagen maturation.
notes.E: Lysosomal proteolysis helps degrade proteins and is distinct from extracellular processing to build collagen fibrils.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts selected lysine residues into reactive allysine for collagen cross-linking?
questions.why: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent extracellular enzyme. It oxidatively deaminates certain lysine residues to allysine, an aldehyde that can participate in covalent cross-links.

notes.A: Prolyl hydroxylase adds hydroxyl groups to selected proline residues rather than making lysine-derived aldehydes.
notes.B: Formation of allysine is oxidative deamination, not transfer of phosphate from ATP.
notes.C: Vitamin K-dependent carboxylase modifies glutamate residues in other proteins, including clotting factors.
notes.D: Procollagen maturation does not use a zinc-dependent ligase to convert lysine to allysine.

questions.stem: At which stage is the final covalent strengthening of collagen fibrils achieved?
questions.why: After collagen molecules assemble outside the cell, lysyl oxidase creates reactive residues that can form covalent links between them. These links give fibrils further tensile strength.

notes.A: Ribosomal synthesis provides the individual chains and does not connect assembled extracellular collagen molecules.
notes.B: Glycine fits into the triple-helix core, but oxidation of glycine inside the cell does not generate the mature fibril cross-links.
notes.D: Retinol is a vitamin A derivative and its metabolism is separate from fibril strengthening.
notes.E: Transcription produces the precursor mRNA and occurs before the protein is available for cross-linking.

questions.stem: Which metal is particularly important for lysyl oxidase-mediated cross-linking?
questions.why: Lysyl oxidase requires copper for catalysis. Its oxidation of selected lysine and hydroxylysine side chains supplies reactive aldehydes for extracellular cross-link formation.

notes.B: Zinc is used by several matrix metalloproteinases but is not the required metal for lysyl oxidase.
notes.C: Sodium helps determine extracellular ion gradients and is not the catalytic metal of this oxidase.
notes.D: Magnesium supports many ATP-dependent enzymes, but lysyl oxidase is copper-dependent.
notes.E: Potassium is important in membrane physiology but does not support this enzyme's oxidative deamination as its metal cofactor.

questions.stem: A patient with poor wound healing and bleeding gums lacks a vitamin needed for collagen hydroxylation. Which condition is likely?
questions.why: Scurvy is vitamin C deficiency. Reduced formation of hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine impairs collagen maturation, helping explain fragile gingival tissues and delayed wound repair.

notes.A: Osteolathyrism involves deficient collagen cross-linking and is not caused by inadequate vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation.
notes.B: Porphyrias involve disturbances in haem synthesis, which do not explain this collagen enzyme defect.
notes.C: Pellagra is niacin deficiency and is classically associated with dermatitis, diarrhoea and neuropsychiatric symptoms.
notes.E: Beriberi is thiamine deficiency and chiefly affects nervous or cardiovascular function.

questions.stem: Which collagen biosynthetic step is specifically impaired in nutritional scurvy?
questions.why: Ascorbate maintains iron in the active state for collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases. Nutritional scurvy therefore impairs hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues on nascent collagen.

notes.A: Propeptide cleavage is a distinct processing step performed by specialised peptidases.
notes.C: Hydroxyproline is formed by modification of peptide-bound proline, rather than inserted directly by ribosomes.
notes.D: Lysyl oxidase requires copper and makes reactive aldehydes at a later extracellular stage.
notes.E: The primary collagen defect is a failure of normal hydroxylation, not failure to translate elastin mRNA.

questions.stem: Which clinical combination is characteristic of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes?
questions.why: Ehlers-Danlos syndromes comprise inherited connective-tissue disorders, often causing joint hypermobility, hyperextensible skin and tissue fragility.

notes.A: Night blindness is a manifestation of rod or visual-cycle dysfunction rather than a defining connective-tissue symptom.
notes.B: Anaemia and raised urate can have metabolic or haematological causes and do not define these syndromes.
notes.C: Tetany is associated with neuromuscular excitability, often from low calcium. Kidney stones are not the defining feature of Ehlers–Danlos syndromes.
notes.D: Jaundice and hepatomegaly are more typical of a hepatic or haematological problem than the classic connective-tissue presentation.

questions.stem: A hereditary defect of type I collagen produces brittle bones and repeated fractures. Which disorder fits best?
questions.why: Osteogenesis imperfecta frequently results from type I collagen abnormalities, including glycine substitutions disrupting the helix.

notes.A: Some Ehlers–Danlos subtypes involve type I collagen, but recurrent fractures and brittle bones are typical of osteogenesis imperfecta.
notes.B: Marfan syndrome typically involves fibrillin-1 and is characterised by skeletal, ocular and cardiovascular findings.
notes.D: Osteolathyrism impairs extracellular cross-linking, rather than representing the usual inherited type I collagen disorder.
notes.E: Dermatoparaxis is a collagen-processing disorder classically associated with severe skin fragility.

questions.stem: Absence of a procollagen peptidase in cattle produces extremely fragile skin. What is the condition called?
questions.why: Dermatoparaxis in cattle reflects deficient removal of the amino-terminal procollagen propeptide. The retained propeptide distorts fibril assembly and makes skin extremely fragile.

notes.B: Osteogenesis imperfecta typically involves abnormalities of type I collagen and presents prominently with bone fragility.
notes.C: Osteolathyrism affects cross-linking through lysyl oxidase inhibition rather than defective cleavage of a procollagen propeptide.
notes.D: Scurvy is vitamin C deficiency, which mainly affects collagen proline and lysine hydroxylation.
notes.E: Pellagra is due to inadequate niacin activity, with dermatitis rather than a specific procollagen peptidase defect.

questions.stem: Which toxin inhibits lysyl oxidase and causes defective collagen cross-linking in lathyrism?
questions.why: In osteolathyrism, beta-aminopropionitrile inhibits lysyl oxidase. This limits formation of the lysine-derived aldehydes needed for normal covalent cross-links in connective tissue.

notes.A: Alpha-alpha-bipyridyl chelates iron and can impair iron-dependent hydroxylation rather than causing this lysyl oxidase defect.
notes.B: Dinitrophenol uncouples oxidative phosphorylation rather than selectively inhibiting connective-tissue cross-linking.
notes.C: Methotrexate inhibits folate-dependent processes and is not the lathyrogen in this question.
notes.E: Isoniazid inhibits mycolic acid synthesis in susceptible mycobacteria and is not the cause of osteolathyrism here.

questions.stem: Which property best distinguishes elastin from collagen in mature tissues?
questions.why: Elastin forms extensible fibres that recoil, while collagen principally provides tensile strength.

notes.A: Collagen is especially effective at resisting tensile deformation. The distinctive elastic-fibre property is returning towards the original shape after stretching.
notes.C: Type IV collagen provides the characteristic sheet-like structural network in basal laminae.
notes.D: A mineralised matrix is characteristic of tissues such as bone, where mineral associates with a collagen-rich framework.
notes.E: Anchoring fibrils consist mainly of type VII collagen and are not elastic fibres.

questions.stem: Which unusual cross-link is especially characteristic of mature elastin?
questions.why: Desmosine links four lysine-derived side chains and is a characteristic covalent cross-link of mature elastin. Along with isodesmosine, it helps stabilise the elastic network.

notes.A: Hydroxyproline is a modified residue especially abundant in collagen and does not itself describe an elastin cross-link.
notes.B: Phosphotyrosine is a phosphorylated amino acid used in signalling, rather than a structural link between elastin chains.
notes.C: Cystathionine is an intermediate of sulphur amino acid metabolism and is not an elastic-fibre cross-link.
notes.D: Selenocysteine occurs in certain selenoproteins but does not form the characteristic covalent links of elastin.

questions.stem: How many lysine residues contribute to one desmosine cross-link in elastin?
questions.why: Desmosine has four lysine-derived arms. Lysyl oxidase generates reactive aldehydes from some of the lysines, allowing condensation into a mature cross-link.

notes.A: Two lysine-derived groups can participate in simpler cross-links but cannot account for all four origins of desmosine.
notes.B: Three contributes too few lysine-derived groups, even though several are oxidised during cross-link formation.
notes.D: Five exceeds the number of lysine residues contributing to the tetrafunctional structure.
notes.E: Six lysines are not required. A single desmosine cross-link derives from four side chains.

questions.stem: Compared with collagen, mature elastin is notable for relatively little of which residue?
questions.why: Elastin contains relatively little hydroxyproline compared with collagen. The high collagen content of this modified residue reflects its role in stabilising the triple helix.

notes.B: Glycine is abundant in elastin as well as in collagen, where it occurs at every third helical position.
notes.C: Proline is a common constituent of elastin. The difference asked about concerns its hydroxylated derivative.
notes.D: Valine is among the hydrophobic residues found extensively in elastin.
notes.E: Alanine is common in the hydrophobic regions of elastin and is not the relevant low-abundance modification.

questions.stem: Which tissue contains abundant elastin because it must expand and recoil with each pulse of blood?
questions.why: The aortic media contains abundant elastic lamellae. They stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, helping maintain forward flow between ventricular ejections.

notes.A: Tooth enamel is highly mineralised to resist wear and is not adapted for repeated pulsatile expansion.
notes.B: The lens is rich in crystallin proteins for transparency rather than elastic lamellae for handling blood pressure.
notes.C: Bone cortex uses mineralised collagen for rigidity and is not adapted to recoil with the arterial pulse.
notes.E: The retinal pigment epithelium supports photoreceptors and does not serve as a pulsatile vessel wall.
